destitute

/DES-tih-toot/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Destitute means extremely poor, lacking even the basic necessities of life.

The wildfire moved so fast that hundreds of families fled with only the clothes they wore, left destitute overnight, without homes, food, or savings.

Example

After three years of drought killed his crops and then his cattle, the farmer sold the last of his tools to pay old debts. Destitute, he arrived in the city with nothing but a blanket and depended on a soup kitchen for his only meal each day.

The farmer has lost not just income but everything, food, shelter, and possessions alike, which is what separates being destitute from being merely poor.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

impoverished: Impoverished means made poor, often by forces that drained resources over time: an impoverished region, an impoverished family. An impoverished household may still have a roof and some income. Destitute is the endpoint: lacking food, shelter, and every basic necessity, with nothing left to fall back on.

poverty-stricken: Poverty-stricken describes people suffering under severe, grinding poverty, usually as a long-standing condition of life. Destitute is even more absolute, and often more sudden: it means stripped of the basics themselves, food, shelter, and savings, the state a disaster can leave a family in overnight.

broke: Broke is the casual, everyday word for having no money at the moment, and it is often temporary: a student can be broke until payday. Destitute is far graver. It means lacking even food and shelter, not just cash, and no one uses it lightly.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

wealthy: having a great deal of money

prosperous: successful and financially thriving

Where it sits · how deep the poverty runs

needy → destitute → penniless

needy vs. destitute: A needy family lacks enough money for comfort but still gets by, while a destitute one lacks food, shelter, and every basic necessity.

penniless vs. destitute: Destitute describes total poverty in daily life, and penniless sharpens it even further, meaning literally not a single cent remains.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-: down, away

Root — stitute: from Latin statuere, to set or place

Put it together: Destitute comes from Latin destituere, 'to abandon, to set down and leave,' built from de-, 'down, away,' plus statuere, 'to set or place.' In the word's original picture, someone destitute has been set down and deserted by fortune, left standing with nothing at all.

Use the root in a new word: statute: A statute is a law formally 'set in place' by a legislature, carrying the same Latin root, statuere, that hides inside destitute.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal

Destitute describes total poverty, the loss of food, shelter, and every basic necessity, and it often appears in the phrase 'left destitute.' Indigent, a related word taught elsewhere in this unit, covers similar poverty in a more clinical, institutional register, as in official discussions of who qualifies for aid, while destitute is the more absolute and dramatic word.
